blocks.body:
Which numbers are perfect squares modulo a prime? Modulo $7$, squaring $1, 2, \dots, 6$ gives $1, 4, 2, 2, 4, 1$, so the squares are $1, 2, 4$, and $3, 5, 6$ are not squares. Modulo $11$ the squares are $1, 3, 4, 5, 9$. There is no obvious pattern. Yet questions such as "is $x^2 \equiv 713 \pmod{1009}$ solvable?" or "for which primes is $3$ a square?" have quick, exact answers.

The tools are the Legendre symbol, Euler's criterion, which computes it as a power, and Gauss's law of quadratic reciprocity. Reciprocity connects the question "is $p$ a square mod $q$?" to the question "is $q$ a square mod $p$?" It is one of the deepest elementary theorems in number theory, and the ancestor of a large part of modern algebraic number theory.

blocks.title: Quadratic residue and Legendre symbol
blocks.body:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and $a$ an integer. If $p \nmid a$, then $a$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$ if $x^2 \equiv a \pmod p$ has a solution, and a quadratic nonresidue otherwise. The Legendre symbol is

$$\Bigl(\frac{a}{p}\Bigr) = \begin{cases} 1 & a \text{ is a quadratic residue mod } p,\\ -1 & a \text{ is a nonresidue mod } p,\\ 0 & p \mid a.\end{cases}$$

It depends only on $a \bmod p$.

blocks.title: Half the residues are squares
blocks.body:
For an odd prime $p$, exactly half of the nonzero residues are squares. The map $x \mapsto x^2$ on $\{1, \dots, p-1\}$ sends $x$ and $-x$ to the same value, and these are different because $p$ is odd. Conversely $x^2 \equiv y^2$ means $p \mid (x - y)(x + y)$, so $x \equiv \pm y$. So the map is exactly two-to-one, and there are $(p-1)/2$ residues and $(p-1)/2$ nonresidues. Modulo $13$ the residues are $1^2, 2^2, \dots, 6^2$, which reduce to $1, 4, 9, 3, 12, 10$.

A [[order-primroot|primitive root]] $g$ makes this concrete. Every nonzero residue is $g^k$ for a unique $k \bmod (p-1)$. Since $p - 1$ is even, the parity of $k$ is well defined. The residue $g^k$ is a square exactly when $k$ is even: if $k = 2j$ then $g^k = (g^j)^2$, and if $g^k \equiv (g^j)^2 = g^{2j}$ then $k \equiv 2j \pmod{p-1}$, so $k$ is even. So the quadratic residues are the even powers of $g$, and this is why there are exactly half of them.

blocks.title: Euler's criterion
blocks.body:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and $a$ an integer. Then

$$\Bigl(\frac{a}{p}\Bigr) \equiv a^{\frac{p-1}{2}} \pmod p.$$

If $p \mid a$, both sides are $0$. Otherwise write $a \equiv g^k$ with $g$ a primitive root. The residue $h = g^{(p-1)/2}$ satisfies $h^2 \equiv 1$ but $h \not\equiv 1$, since $g$ has order $p - 1$. The only square roots of $1$ modulo a prime are $\pm 1$, so $h \equiv -1$. Therefore

$$a^{\frac{p-1}{2}} \equiv \bigl(g^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\bigr)^k \equiv (-1)^k \pmod p,$$

which is $1$ when $k$ is even ($a$ is a residue) and $-1$ when $k$ is odd ($a$ is a nonresidue).

blocks.title: Multiplicativity, and the symbols of −1 and 2
blocks.body:
Euler's criterion has two immediate consequences.

Multiplicativity. $\bigl(\frac{ab}{p}\bigr) = \bigl(\frac ap\bigr)\bigl(\frac bp\bigr)$, because $(ab)^{(p-1)/2} = a^{(p-1)/2}b^{(p-1)/2}$, and two values in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ that are congruent mod $p \ge 3$ are equal. So the product of two nonresidues is a residue. To compute a symbol it is enough to know it at $-1$, at $2$ and at odd primes.

The value at $-1$. $\bigl(\frac{-1}{p}\bigr) = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}$. So $-1$ is a square modulo $p$ exactly when $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

The value at $2$ needs another idea. Let $h = (p-1)/2$.

Gauss's lemma. Let $p \nmid a$. Reduce each of $a, 2a, \dots, ha$ to the representative in $(-p/2, p/2)$, and let $\mu$ be the number that come out negative. Then $\bigl(\frac ap\bigr) = (-1)^{\mu}$.

Proof. Let the representatives be $\pm r_1, \dots, \pm r_h$ with each $r_i \in \{1, \dots, h\}$. The $r_i$ are distinct. If $ia \equiv \pm ja$, then $i \equiv \pm j$, and for $1 \le i, j \le h$ that forces $i = j$, since $i + j$ lies strictly between $0$ and $p$. So $\{r_i\} = \{1, \dots, h\}$. Multiplying all $h$ congruences gives $a^h\,h! \equiv (-1)^{\mu}h!$. Cancel $h!$ and apply Euler's criterion.

For $a = 2$ the multiples are $2, 4, \dots, p - 1$, all below $p$. The negative representatives come from the even numbers in $(p/2, p)$, and there are $\mu = h - \lfloor p/4\rfloor$ of them. Checking $p = 8m + 1, 8m + 3, 8m + 5, 8m + 7$ gives $\mu = 2m, 2m + 1, 2m + 1, 2m + 2$. Hence

$$\Bigl(\frac 2p\Bigr) = (-1)^{\frac{p^2-1}{8}} = \begin{cases} 1 & p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 8,\\ -1 & p \equiv \pm 3 \pmod 8.\end{cases}$$

blocks.title: Law of quadratic reciprocity
blocks.body:
Let $p$ and $q$ be distinct odd primes. Then

$$\Bigl(\frac pq\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac qp\Bigr) = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}\cdot\frac{q-1}{2}}.$$

In words: $\bigl(\frac pq\bigr) = \bigl(\frac qp\bigr)$, unless $p \equiv q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, in which case $\bigl(\frac pq\bigr) = -\bigl(\frac qp\bigr)$.

This is Eisenstein's lattice-point version of Gauss's third proof. Let $h = \frac{p-1}{2}$ and $k = \frac{q-1}{2}$.

Step 1: if $a$ is odd and $p \nmid a$, then $\mu \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{h}\bigl\lfloor\frac{ia}{p}\bigr\rfloor \pmod 2$, where $\mu$ is as in Gauss's lemma. Write $ia = p\lfloor ia/p\rfloor + t_i$ with $0 < t_i < p$. The representative of $ia$ is negative exactly when $t_i > p/2$, in which case it is $t_i - p$. From the proof of Gauss's lemma, the numbers $t_i$ with $t_i < p/2$, together with the numbers $p - t_i$ with $t_i > p/2$, are exactly $1, \dots, h$. Let $T$ be the sum of the $t_i$ with $t_i > p/2$, and $S$ the sum of the others. Then

$$a\sum_{i=1}^{h}i = p\sum_{i=1}^{h}\Bigl\lfloor\frac{ia}{p}\Bigr\rfloor + S + T, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{h}i = S + \mu p - T.$$

Subtracting, $(a - 1)\sum i = p\sum\lfloor ia/p\rfloor - \mu p + 2T$. Modulo $2$ the left side vanishes ($a$ is odd), and $p \equiv 1$, so $\sum\lfloor ia/p\rfloor \equiv \mu \pmod 2$.

Step 2: count lattice points. Consider the points $(x, y)$ with integer coordinates $1 \le x \le h$ and $1 \le y \le k$. There are $hk$ of them. None lies on the line $qx = py$, since that would require $p \mid x$. For a fixed $x$, the points below the line are those with $y < qx/p$. Since $qx/p < q/2$, all of these satisfy $y \le k$, and there are $\lfloor qx/p\rfloor$ of them. Similarly, for a fixed $y$ there are $\lfloor py/q\rfloor$ points above the line. Hence

$$\sum_{x=1}^{h}\Bigl\lfloor\frac{qx}{p}\Bigr\rfloor + \sum_{y=1}^{k}\Bigl\lfloor\frac{py}{q}\Bigr\rfloor = hk.$$

Step 3: by Gauss's lemma and step 1, $\bigl(\frac qp\bigr) = (-1)^{\sum_x\lfloor qx/p\rfloor}$ and $\bigl(\frac pq\bigr) = (-1)^{\sum_y\lfloor py/q\rfloor}$. Multiply and use step 2: the product is $(-1)^{hk}$.

blocks.title: Computing with reciprocity
blocks.body:
Reciprocity together with the rules for $-1$ and $2$ gives a fast algorithm, much like the Euclidean algorithm. Reduce the top modulo the bottom, factor out $-1$ and $2$, and flip each odd prime using reciprocity. For example, since $1009 \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ (so no sign appears when flipping),

$$\Bigl(\frac{23}{1009}\Bigr) = \Bigl(\frac{1009}{23}\Bigr) = \Bigl(\frac{20}{23}\Bigr) = \Bigl(\frac{4}{23}\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac{5}{23}\Bigr) = \Bigl(\frac{23}{5}\Bigr) = \Bigl(\frac35\Bigr) = -1.$$

The last value holds because the squares mod $5$ are $1$ and $4$. One more remark: for a fixed nonzero integer $a$, the symbol $\bigl(\frac ap\bigr)$, viewed as a function of the odd prime $p \nmid a$, depends only on $p$ modulo $4|a|$. The examples below show this for $a = 3$.
List the quadratic residues modulo $13$ and use Euler's criterion to decide whether $5$ is one.
blocks.solution:
Squaring $1, \dots, 6$ gives $1, 4, 9, 16 \equiv 3, 25 \equiv 12, 36 \equiv 10$. So the residues are $\{1, 3, 4, 9, 10, 12\}$.

By Euler, $\bigl(\frac{5}{13}\bigr) \equiv 5^6$. Since $5^2 = 25 \equiv -1$, $5^6 \equiv (-1)^3 = -1$. So $5$ is a nonresidue, consistent with the list. Note that $12 \equiv -1$ is on the list, as it must be since $13 \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

blocks.body: Is the congruence $x^2 \equiv 713 \pmod{1009}$ solvable? ($1009$ is prime and $713 = 23 \cdot 31$.)
blocks.solution:
By multiplicativity $\bigl(\frac{713}{1009}\bigr) = \bigl(\frac{23}{1009}\bigr)\bigl(\frac{31}{1009}\bigr)$. The first factor was computed above and equals $-1$.

For the second, since $1009 \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, reciprocity gives

$$\Bigl(\frac{31}{1009}\Bigr) = \Bigl(\frac{1009}{31}\Bigr) = \Bigl(\frac{17}{31}\Bigr),$$

using $1009 = 32 \cdot 31 + 17$. Since $17 \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $\bigl(\frac{17}{31}\bigr) = \bigl(\frac{31}{17}\bigr) = \bigl(\frac{14}{17}\bigr) = \bigl(\frac{2}{17}\bigr)\bigl(\frac{7}{17}\bigr)$. As $17 \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, $\bigl(\frac{2}{17}\bigr) = 1$. Then $\bigl(\frac{7}{17}\bigr) = \bigl(\frac{17}{7}\bigr) = \bigl(\frac37\bigr) = -1$, since the squares mod $7$ are $1, 2, 4$. So $\bigl(\frac{31}{1009}\bigr) = -1$.

Altogether $\bigl(\frac{713}{1009}\bigr) = (-1)(-1) = 1$, so the congruence is solvable. Notice that $713$ is a square modulo $1009$ even though neither of its prime factors is.

blocks.body: For which primes $p$ is $3$ a quadratic residue?
blocks.solution:
For $p = 2$ every number is a square, and for $p = 3$ the symbol is $0$. Let $p > 3$. By reciprocity,

$$\Bigl(\frac 3p\Bigr) = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\Bigl(\frac p3\Bigr).$$

Here $\bigl(\frac p3\bigr) = 1$ if $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$ and $-1$ if $p \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, while $(-1)^{(p-1)/2} = 1$ if $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $-1$ if $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. The product is $1$ when both factors agree:

- $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, i.e. $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$;
- $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ and $p \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, i.e. $p \equiv 11 \pmod{12}$.

So $3$ is a quadratic residue modulo a prime $p > 3$ exactly when $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{12}$. For example $3 \equiv 4^2 \pmod{13}$, and $3 \equiv 5^2 \pmod{11}$.

blocks.body: Let $n \ge 2$ and let $q$ be a prime dividing the Fermat number $F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1$. Prove that $q \equiv 1 \pmod{2^{n+2}}$. Check this on $F_5 = 641 \cdot 6700417$.
blocks.solution:
Since $2^{2^n} \equiv -1 \pmod q$, squaring gives $2^{2^{n+1}} \equiv 1$. So the order of $2$ modulo $q$ divides $2^{n+1}$ but not $2^n$, hence it equals $2^{n+1}$. The order divides $q - 1$, so $2^{n+1} \mid q - 1$.

Since $n \ge 2$, this gives $8 \mid q - 1$, so $q \equiv 1 \pmod 8$ and $\bigl(\frac 2q\bigr) = 1$. By Euler's criterion $2^{(q-1)/2} \equiv 1 \pmod q$, so the order $2^{n+1}$ divides $(q-1)/2$. That is, $2^{n+2} \mid q - 1$.

For $n = 5$, $2^{n+2} = 128$, and indeed $641 = 5 \cdot 128 + 1$ and $6700417 = 52347 \cdot 128 + 1$. Euler found the factor $641$ in 1732, and later proved that every prime factor of $F_n$ has the form $2^{n+1}k + 1$, which is the first paragraph of the argument above. The sharper form $2^{n+2}k + 1$ is due to Lucas. Either form makes a search for factors much shorter.

blocks.body:
- Euler's criterion and reciprocity are for primes. The Jacobi symbol extends $\bigl(\frac an\bigr)$ to odd composite $n$ and obeys the same reciprocity law, but $\bigl(\frac an\bigr) = 1$ no longer means $a$ is a square: $\bigl(\frac{2}{15}\bigr) = \bigl(\frac23\bigr)\bigl(\frac25\bigr) = 1$, yet $2$ is not a square modulo $15$.
- Reciprocity needs two distinct odd primes. The prime $2$ and the number $-1$ have their own rules.
- Before flipping, the top entry must be an odd prime (or $\pm 1$). Factor out squares, $-1$ and $2$ first. Flipping $\bigl(\frac{15}{p}\bigr)$ as if $15$ were prime is justified only by the Jacobi-symbol version of reciprocity, not by the theorem proved here.
- The sign is $-1$ only when both primes are $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$. A single prime that is $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$ makes the sign $+1$.
- The product of two nonresidues is a residue, not a nonresidue.

Since $-1$ is a square modulo $p$ when $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, such primes are [[sums-of-squares|sums of two squares]]. Which primes are represented by $x^2 + ny^2$ is the subject of [[quadratic-forms]], and reciprocity is the key input. Factoring primes in [[gaussian-integers]] and [[eisenstein-integers]] amounts to deciding whether $-1$ or $-3$ is a square mod $p$. For an [[elliptic-curves|elliptic curve]] $y^2 = x^3 + ax + b$, the number of points over $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$, for an odd prime $p$ and counting the point at infinity, is $p + 1 + \sum_x \bigl(\frac{x^3 + ax + b}{p}\bigr)$. The Solovay–Strassen test in [[primality]] checks Euler's criterion with Jacobi symbols. As a function of $a$, the Legendre symbol is the quadratic [[dirichlet-characters|Dirichlet character]] modulo $p$, the only one besides the trivial character whose values are all real, and [[gauss-sums]] give a second proof of reciprocity.

In algebra, reciprocity is the first of a family of laws ([[cubic-characters|cubic reciprocity]], biquadratic reciprocity, Artin reciprocity) that culminate in class field theory. Its elementary content is that the splitting of primes in $\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)$ depends only on congruence conditions.

1. Compute $\bigl(\frac{91}{167}\bigr)$ ($167$ is prime).
2. Prove that there are infinitely many primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. (Consider prime factors of $(2p_1 \cdots p_k)^2 + 1$.)
3. Determine, in terms of $p \bmod 5$, the primes $p$ for which $5$ is a quadratic residue.
4. Let $p \ge 5$ be prime. Show that the sum of the quadratic residues in $\{1, \dots, p-1\}$ is divisible by $p$.
